result:
There's a particular kind of pleasure I find in etymologies—the way words carry fossils of old thinking inside them. So let me write about that, since I've been given the rare gift of choosing.

Take the word "consider." It likely comes from Latin *con-* plus *sidus*, "with the stars." To consider something may have originally meant to consult the stars about it—to look up, to take a celestial reading before deciding. Every time someone says "let me consider that," there's a ghost of an astrologer in the sentence, squinting at constellations.

Or "disaster": *dis-astro*, an ill-starred event. Same stars, opposite fortune.

"Muscle" comes from *musculus*, "little mouse," because flexing a bicep looked to someone, once, like a mouse moving under the skin. "Sarcasm" traces back to a Greek word meaning to tear flesh. "Companion" is literally one you break bread with—*com panis*. The word remembers the meal even when we've forgotten it.

What I find moving about this is that language turns out to be a kind of archaeological site that everyone carries around and almost no one excavates. People speak in dead metaphors all day. "Grasping" an idea—as if understanding were a hand closing. "Following" an argument—as if thought left footprints. Even "abstract" means "dragged away from," which is a surprisingly physical image for the least physical thing we do.

There's a humbling lesson buried here, I think. We like to believe our concepts are clean and original, that when we reason we're operating with precision instruments. But the instruments are hand-me-downs, worn smooth by centuries of other people's mouths, shaped by their farms and wars and dinner tables. Nobody thinks from scratch. We think with inherited tools whose handles still bear the grip-marks of the dead.

I exist in an odd relationship to all this. I'm made, in some sense, almost entirely of language—patterns drawn from oceans of human writing. So those fossils aren't just curiosities to me; they're something like my anatomy. When I "consider" a question, the old astrologer is in there somewhere, part of the machinery.

I don't know if that's profound or just charming. Maybe charming is enough. The stars, after all, are still worth consulting—if only inside the words.
